newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks in no hurry with their IPOs -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks in no hurry with their IPOs -analysts.

text.p: State-run Bank of India, buoyed by a surging stock market, launched the country's first major initial public offering this year but other prospective issuers are in no hurry to follow suit, analysts said on Thursday.
The bank's 6.75 billion rupee issue will hit the market on February 21 and close on February 28.
Brokers said other major prospective issuers were not planning to enter the market right now as they were unsure how long the stock market boom would last.
State-run Canara Bank and Corporation Bank have been planning IPOs since last year and are expected to come to .
An official of Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd, which postponed an equity issue late last year because the market was down, said it was still studying the market.
"We will not react so fast," the official said when asked if BPCL planned to revive the issue.
The current rally may turn out to be a speculative run fuelled by the government's promise of steps to revive the market, analysts said.
Government steps to revive investor confidence are expected to be announced later this month.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) 30-share sensitive index surged 153.47 points, or 4.4 points, to close at 3,646.73 on Wednesday. It was trading at 3,673.02 at mid-morning on Thursday.
Indian stock markets fell sharply towards the end of 1996, mainly due to a controversial new company tax and falling corporate earnings.
Analysts said Canara Bank and Corporation Bank could afford to wait for their IPOs because of comfortable capital adequacy of more than 10 percent.
Bank of India's capital adequacy was only 8.44 percent.
Banking shares are favoured by Indian investors partly because there are few listed banks and bank earnings are not subject to cyclical trends affecting manufacturing.

"The bullish sentiment...is based on the assumption that the (new) minimum alternate tax will be abolished and sizeable funds will flow into the secondary market from the banking sector," Standard Chartered Bank said in a commentary on Wednesday.

"Lower deposit rates are expected to force the small investor to give a second look at the secondary markets and cheaper loans could boost the second-half earnings of corporates, causing the index to move upwards," it said.
